content: Writing differs significantly from speaking. When speaking, one can use expressions such as changes in voice tone, volume, pauses, hesitations, or even facial and hand gestures to convey meaning. However, in writing, these non-verbal cues are absent, and the words appear flat on the page. To bring written words to life, punctuation marks are essential. These include the full stop, question mark, exclamation mark, comma, colon, semicolon, dash, and brackets. Full Stop Every sentence, whether short or long, must end with a full stop (period). Full stops are used to conclude complete sentences. A single long sentence can convey as much information as several shorter ones. Effective writing often combines short, medium, and long sentences. Example: The management of a patient with acute decompensated heart failure depends on whether the patient has acute decompensated systolic heart failure or acute decompensated diastolic heart failure. Question Mark Sentences that ask a question end with a question mark. Like all sentences, they begin with a capital letter. Example: Is the patient symptomatic? Exclamation Mark Exclamation marks are used to express strong emotions such as anger, surprise, urgency, amusement, or annoyance. They can also emphasize short commands, which may consist of just one word. Example: Thank you. Comma Commas make sentences, especially longer ones, easier to read. When reading aloud, commas often indicate a slight pause or change in tone. They are frequently used when naming or describing something. Always remember to include a space after a comma. Commas also help connect phrases or clauses within a sentence. Examples: Oxygen improves the patient’s status if hypoxemia is present, and the goal is to keep the oxygen saturation above 90%. Following transmission, the agent inoculates the tracheobronchial epithelium. During a streptococcal infection, activated antigen-presenting cells such as macrophages, present the bacterial antigen to helper T cells. Semicolon A semicolon indicates a stronger break than a comma but does not replace a full stop. It can connect two related sentences or parts of a sentence. Use semicolons when the sentences are closely related or belong together. Example: The most recent classification according to the left ventricular ejection fraction; heart failure with reduced ejection fraction vs. heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, is widely used. Colon A colon is used to introduce a list, provide examples, or clarify a preceding statement. It can also appear before instructions or explanations. Examples: There are numerous systemic risk factors associated with thrombus formation following plaque rupture: Smoking: Smoking increases platelet aggregation and plasma epinephrine levels. Fibrinogen: Elevated levels of fibrinogen have been associated with thrombosis, including abnormal levels of fibrinogen. Brackets Brackets are used in pairs to include additional information that may be helpful but is not essential to the main sentence. Example: Atherosclerosis is the gradual buildup of cholesterol and fibrous tissue (collagen and smooth muscle cells) throughout the vascular tree. Dash Dashes can indicate a significant break or interruption in a sentence. They may replace colons or brackets and are particularly useful in writing speech or showing interruptions. Example: Pathology studies indicate that it is often mild-to-moderate, lipid-laden, inflamed plaques that are the ones most likely to rupture and cause an ST elevation MI. Capitalization The first word of every sentence or bullet point should begin with a capital letter. Proper nouns, such as names of people, places, or specific things, are also capitalized regardless of their position in a sentence. Examples: Heart failure is defined as the inability of the heart to pump enough blood to meet the demands of the body. The patient is suffering from Münchausen syndrome but has no symptoms of major depressive disorder. The preferred drug for the symptoms of this disease is Tylenol, which contains acetaminophen. Chickenpox is caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV). A study conducted in Olmsted County, Minnesota, showed that the incidence of heart failure (ICD 9/428) has not declined during two decades, but survival after onset has increased overall. Apostrophes Apostrophes indicate possession or contractions. For singular words, use ‘s, even if the word ends in –s. For plural words ending in –s, place the apostrophe after the s. For irregular plurals, use ‘s. Avoid placing apostrophes in simple plurals. Examples: The patient’s heart Ankles’ bones Appendix’s entries Bullet Points Bullet points help organize information into clear, concise chunks. They are often indented and double-spaced in academic writing. The text introducing the list should end with a colon, and the first word of each bullet point is typically capitalized. Example: Activated antigen-presenting cells, such as macrophages. Special Cases of Capitalization in Titles In titles, capitalize all words except articles (a, an, the), short conjunctions (and, as, but, if, or, nor), and short prepositions (at, by, for, in, of, on, to, up). However, always capitalize the first and last words of a title, as well as the first word following a dash or colon. Examples: Retinal Hemangioblastoma in von Hippel–Lindau Disease Autism in Children Born After In Vitro Fertilization Referencing References should be placed at the end of a sentence, following the period. Example: Acute or decompensated heart failure refers to an episode in which a patient sustains a change in heart failure signs and symptoms that necessitate urgent therapy or hospitalization. Additional Editing Help Grammarly is a useful tool for reviewing spelling, punctuation, and grammar. It can be used as a browser extension or a standalone app. It highlights errors and suggests corrections in real-time. Editors should ensure that content adheres to standardized templates and avoid accepting non-standardized suggestions.
